## United States Court of Appeals, Fifth Circuit.
### No. 25-40026

### Decided: July 21, 2026

### Before Higginbotham, Smith, and Oldham, Circuit Judges.
## United States Court of Appeals, Fifth Circuit.
Concepcion Palomares was charged with unlawful possession of a firearm as a felon in violation of 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(1). The count was predicated on his conviction of transporting illegal aliens. The district court dismissed the count as violative of the Second Amendment. The government appeals.

 We reverse and remand.
Palomares filed a motion to dismiss that count, contending that it violated the Second Amendment as applied to him.^1 The government asserted that disarmament based on a § 1324(a)(1)(A)(ii) conviction is consistent with the Second Amendment because slave smuggling was a capital offense at the Founding.

# UNITED STATES v. PALOMARES (2022)
## United States Court of Appeals, Fifth Circuit.
### No. 21-40247

### Decided: November 02, 2022

### Before Jolly, Willett, and Oldham, Circuit Judges.
## United States Court of Appeals, Fifth Circuit.
The district court sentenced appellant Nonami Palomares to a 120-month “mandatory minimum” sentence for smuggling heroin. She argues the district court erred because 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f), more commonly referred to as the First Step Act's “safety valve” provision, exempts drug offenders like Palomares, with sufficiently minor criminal histories from mandatory minimum sentences.
The relevant part of the statute states that criminal defendants are eligible for relief only if:

(1) the defendant does not have—

(A) more than 4 criminal history points, excluding any criminal history points resulting from a 1-point offense, as determined under the sentencing guidelines;

(B) a prior 3-point offense, as determined under the sentencing guidelines; and

(C) a prior 2-point violent offense, as determined under the sentencing guidelines[.]
18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)(1). Palomares argues that she was eligible for relief because her criminal history only ran afoul of sub-section (B)—she had a prior 3-point offense. Because the statute uses the word “and,” she argues that she would only be ineligible if her criminal history satisfied sub-sections (A), (B), and (C).
To be eligible for safety valve relief, a defendant must show that she does not have more than 4 criminal history points, does not have a 3-point offense, and does not have a 2-point violent offense. Because Palomares had a previous 3-point offense, she is ineligible for safety valve relief. We AFFIRM.

exa-lite.snippet: 25-40026 Like drug trafficking, alien smuggling under § 1324(a)(1)(A)(ii) is “inherently dangerous and often results in death and injury to both aliens and government agents.” United States v. Mendez, 431 F.3d 420, 428 (5th Cir. 2005) (citation omitted). Much of the human-smuggling business along the Mexico border is controlled by drug-trafficking cartels. 3 Cartels use “increased violence to maintain, and seize, new international trade routes and corridors in order to facilitate the international transportation of contraband and immigrants.” 4 Smuggled aliens often face exploitation in the form of “theft, assault, threats, kidnapping (to extort more money), or ransom.” 5 And the transportation itself is often dangerous, as traffickers routinely cram numerous aliens into trunks or engine compartments. ... Mateo Garza, 541 F.3d 290, 293–94 (5th Cir. ... In recognition of those dangers, the U.S. Sentencing Commission has promulgated several sentencing enhancements for alien smuggling. ... § 2L1.1(b)(1–9). Garcia-Guerrero, 313 F.3d 892, 896 (5th Cir. 2002) (quotation omitted). ... Kimble, 142 F.4th at 318. ... 6 We REVERSE the dismissal of Count One and REMAND. - The defendant, Nonami Palomares, pleaded guilty to possession with intent to distribute a significant quantity of heroin, which carried a mandatory minimum sentence of ten years.

REVERSED and REMANDED. (July 21, 2026).
The Fifth Circuit reverses a District Court order dismissing a felon-in-possession charge under 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(1) that had been predicated on Concepcion Palomares’s prior conviction for transporting illegal aliens in violation of 8 U.S.C. § 1324(a)(1)(A)(ii). The Court holds that alien smuggling is an “inherently dangerous felony” that the Government may constitutionally use to disarm a convicted offender consistent with the Second Amendment. Applying the historical-tradition framework from N.Y. State Rifle & Pistol Ass’n, Inc. v. Bruen, 597 U.S. 1 (2022), and its own precedent in United States v. Diaz, 116 F.4th 458 (5th Cir. 2024), the Court, in reliance on United States v. Kimble, 142 F.4th 308 (5th Cir. 2025) (which upheld disarmament of drug traffickers) reasoned that alien smuggling, like drug trafficking, is “notoriously linked to violence” given cartel involvement, exploitation of migrants, and dangerous transport methods. Accordingly, it concludes that Congress’s decision to disarm convicted alien traffickers via § 922(g)(1) does not violate the Second Amendment. Hence, the Court reverses the judgment of the District Court and remands for further proceedings.

## Description of United States v. Palomares: Disarming Convicted Alien Smugglers

In the case of United States v. Palomares, the Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals addressed whether a felon convicted of transporting illegal aliens can be permanently barred from firearm ownership. While a lower district court initially dismissed the gun possession charges as unconstitutional, the appellate court reversed that decision. The judges determined that alien smuggling constitutes an inherently dangerous felony, placing it within a historical tradition of disarming individuals perceived as threats to public safety. By comparing the risks of human trafficking to those of drug trafficking, the court concluded that the government may legally restrict the Second Amendment rights of such offenders. The ruling emphasizes that the legislative and judicial branches view these crimes as notoriously linked to violence, justifying lifetime disarmament. Consequently, the case was remanded for further proceedings, upholding the federal ban on firearm possession for this class of felons.
